# LOD Selection and Culling

Also called: Level-of-Detail Selection, Hierarchical Culling, Multi-resolution Approximation

## Overview
LOD Selection and Culling is the family of methods that dynamically determine the appropriate spatial resolution for rendering volumetric data based on view-dependent metrics (such as distance, projected size, or screen footprint) and hardware constraints [S1][S2, unofficial]. It solves the performance bottleneck of rendering large volumetric datasets by discarding invisible subregions and rendering visible regions at resolutions proportional to their visual importance [S1][S2, unofficial]. It sets itself apart from sibling methods like [Mesh Simplification](1032-mesh-simplification.md) by operating on volumetric primitives ([voxels, bricks](#5794-voxel-bricks.md), splats) rather than surface meshes, and from [Wavelet-based Volume Rendering](1052-wavelet-based-volume-rendering.md) by focusing on the selection logic and culling of pre-existing or generated resolution levels rather than the [decomposition](#7254-decomposition.md) mechanism itself.

## Shared principles
All methods in this family share the core mechanism of generating a hierarchy of data representations at different spatial resolutions [S2, unofficial]. This hierarchy is typically constructed using one of two approaches:
1.  **Spatial Hierarchies:** Structures like Octrees or Bricks that partition the volume domain into sub-regions of varying sizes [S2, unofficial].
2.  **Frequency-Domain Transforms:** Methods like Wavelets that decompose data into coefficients representing different spatial frequencies [S2, unofficial].

Common mathematical and structural operations include:
*   **Scaling Factors:** Defining a scale factor $s$ such that the new resolution $N_{new}$ relates to the previous resolution $N_{prev}$ by $N_{new} = s \times N_{prev}$ or $N_{new} / N_{prev} = s$ [S1, S5, unofficial].
*   **Interpolation and Filtering:** Using interpolation kernels (e.g., trilinear) or filtering to estimate values at new grid points or to generate coarser levels from finer ones [S1][S2, unofficial].
*   **Selection and Culling:** Dynamically choosing which resolution level to render based on spatial hierarchy (distant or less important regions) and hardware constraints [S1][S2, unofficial].

## Subtopics

### [Hierarchical Culling & Multi-resolution Approximation](2010-hierarchical-culling-multi-resolution-approximation.md)
This method accelerates volume rendering by combining spatial culling with multi-resolution data approximation. It solves the performance bottleneck of rendering large volumetric datasets by discarding invisible subregions and rendering visible regions at resolutions proportional to their screen importance. It differs from sibling methods like [Streaming and Level-of-Detail (LOD) selection](3087-streaming-and-level-of-detail-lod-selection.md) by explicitly coupling frustum culling with hardware-assisted [cell projection](#26-cell-projection.md) for exploration, and from [Focus Point Based Brick LOD Selection](5282-focus-point-based-brick-lod-selection.md) by using a global projected size threshold rather than a specific focus point for LOD selection. See [Hierarchical Culling & Multi-resolution Approximation](2010-hierarchical-culling-multi-resolution-approximation.md).

### [Streaming and Level-of-Detail (LOD) selection](3087-streaming-and-level-of-detail-lod-selection.md)
[Streaming and Level-of-Detail (LOD) selection](#3087-streaming-and-level-of-detail-lod-selection.md) is a method for visualizing massive scenes that exceed rendering or memory budgets by dynamically selecting data resolution based on viewpoint position and screen footprint. It solves the problem of navigating arbitrarily large datasets without stalling the frame rate or exceeding memory limits by combining additive ladders (progressive detail) with substitutive levels (coarse approximations) and spatial culling. It sets itself apart from its siblings by explicitly managing the temporal aspect of data arrival and resolution selection through a "level-of-detail grammar" that prioritizes visual coverage preservation during streaming, whereas methods like [Hierarchical Culling & Multi-resolution Approximation](2010-hierarchical-culling-multi-resolution-approximation.md) focus on static hierarchy traversal, and [Focus Point Based Brick LOD Selection](5282-focus-point-based-brick-lod-selection.md) relies on fixed spatial bricks rather than splat-based footprints. See [Streaming and Level-of-Detail (LOD) selection](3087-streaming-and-level-of-detail-lod-selection.md).

### [Focus Point Based Brick LOD Selection](5282-focus-point-based-brick-lod-selection.md)
[Focus Point Based Brick LOD Selection](#5282-focus-point-based-brick-lod-selection.md) is a method to determine the appropriate level-of-detail (LOD) for each brick in a multiscale volume representation based on the distance of the brick's center to a user-defined focus point. It differs from error-driven siblings like [Hierarchical Culling & Multi-resolution Approximation](2010-hierarchical-culling-multi-resolution-approximation.md) because it relies exclusively on geometric proximity to the focus point, ignoring approximation error. This allows for arbitrary texture resolutions per brick, unlike methods with strict texture-to-geometry correspondence. See [Focus Point Based Brick LOD Selection](5282-focus-point-based-brick-lod-selection.md).

### [Choosing Alternative Resolutions](5314-choosing-alternative-resolutions.md)
This method selects a cache-resident resolution level for a volume rendering brick when the desired resolution is not available in memory. It leverages a bitmap of partially mapped resolutions stored in each residency-octree node to efficiently identify candidate levels without random searching. The approach prioritizes lower resolutions before attempting higher ones, iterating through candidates until a mapped page is found or all options are exhausted. See [Choosing Alternative Resolutions](5314-choosing-alternative-resolutions.md).

### [Finding Higher Resolution Levels](5315-finding-higher-resolution-levels.md)
This method finds the next higher resolution level in a [residency octree](#4950-residency-octree.md) traversal where a node is partially mapped. It returns the index of the finest available resolution level strictly higher than a given resolution index, based on a node's occupancy bitmap. It differs from sibling methods that generate data or make final rendering decisions by performing a specific bitwise lookup during [hierarchical traversal](#896-hierarchical-traversal.md). See [Finding Higher Resolution Levels](5315-finding-higher-resolution-levels.md).

### [Multi-resolution LOD Volume Rendering with Temporal Coherence](5717-multi-resolution-lod-volume-rendering-with-temporal-coherenc.md)
[Multi-resolution LOD Volume Rendering with Temporal Coherence](#5717-multi-resolution-lod-volume-rendering-with-temporal-coherenc.md) assigns different resolution levels to subvolumes based on visual importance metrics (projection area, gaze distance, or viewer proximity) to optimize rendering performance while maintaining visual quality. It distinguishes itself from standard LOD methods by explicitly preventing flickering during view changes through a temporal coherence mechanism that stabilizes resolution assignments across consecutive frames. Unlike [Hierarchical Culling & Multi-resolution Approximation](2010-hierarchical-culling-multi-resolution-approximation.md) which may rely on strict hierarchical traversal, this method allows arbitrary texture resolutions for subvolumes provided level transitions are constrained to at most one step per frame. See [Multi-resolution LOD Volume Rendering with Temporal Coherence](5717-multi-resolution-lod-volume-rendering-with-temporal-coherenc.md).

### [Face Subsampling](6025-face-subsampling.md)
[Face Subsampling](#6025-face-subsampling.md) is a Level-of-Detail (LOD) technique for [tetrahedral volume rendering](#820-tetrahedral-volume-rendering.md) that dynamically selects a subset of mesh faces to render, balancing visual fidelity against frame rate constraints. It solves the problem of interactive rendering on large tetrahedral meshes by reducing the number of rasterized primitives without pre-aggregating data into voxels or bricks. It differs from sibling methods like [Hierarchical Culling & Multi-resolution Approximation](2010-hierarchical-culling-multi-resolution-approximation.md) by operating directly on the unstructured mesh topology rather than a hierarchical grid, and from [Focus Point Based Brick LOD Selection](5282-focus-point-based-brick-lod-selection.md) by being primarily face-centric rather than brick-centric. See [Face Subsampling](6025-face-subsampling.md).

### [Flat blocking multi-resolution volume rendering](6428-flat-blocking-multi-resolution-volume-rendering.md)
[Flat blocking multi-resolution volume rendering](#6428-flat-blocking-multi-resolution-volume-rendering.md) is a strategy for loading and rendering large volume datasets by dividing the volume into sub-blocks of equal physical size but assigning each block a different resolution (Level of Detail, LOD) based on its internal data variation. It solves the problem of memory bandwidth and rendering time for large volumes by avoiding uniform high-resolution storage. Unlike hierarchical structures that change spatial extent, this method keeps block dimensions constant while varying the [voxel count](#2908-grid-resolution-calculation.md) within them. It is distinguished from its siblings by its explicit use of a "flat" blocking structure where LOD is determined per block via a variation heuristic, often implemented using min/max octrees. See [Flat blocking multi-resolution volume rendering](6428-flat-blocking-multi-resolution-volume-rendering.md).

### [Level of Detail (LoD) for Large-Scale Scenes](7325-level-of-detail-lod-for-large-scale-scenes.md)
[Level of Detail (LoD) for Large-Scale Scenes](#7325-level-of-detail-lod-for-large-scale-scenes.md) is a technique that regulates the amount of detail needed to represent large-scale scenes by precomputing several simplified versions of the dataset. It solves the problem of rendering massive volumes efficiently by selecting the most appropriate resolution level at runtime based on criteria such as distance to the viewer. Unlike continuous LOD methods, this approach uses discrete, static representations, which are easier to precompute and impose very little overhead at runtime, making it highly suitable for graphics hardware that favors display lists or vertex arrays. See [Level of Detail (LoD) for Large-Scale Scenes](7325-level-of-detail-lod-for-large-scale-scenes.md).

### [Level of Detail Calculation](7836-level-of-detail-calculation.md)
[Level of Detail Calculation](#7836-level-of-detail-calculation.md) determines the specific resolution level $L$ to sample from a multiresolution hierarchy for a given geometric primitive or view ray. It solves the problem of mapping continuous spatial or view-dependent metrics to discrete integer levels in a mip-chain or voxel hierarchy. It sets itself apart from sibling methods by providing the fundamental mathematical mapping function that converts a raw metric (such as projected width) into a fractional level index, which is then split into integer and fractional components for interpolation or selection. See [Level of Detail Calculation](7836-level-of-detail-calculation.md).

### [GPU-Based Dynamic LOD Calculation](10845-gpu-based-dynamic-lod-calculation.md)
This method calculates Level-of-Detail (LOD) levels for visible tiles entirely on the GPU using compute shaders, replacing traditional CPU-side computation based on viewpoint distance and screen-space error. It distinguishes itself by integrating terrain ruggedness into the LOD decision logic and performing the calculation in parallel for thousands of tiles, thereby reducing [CPU](#10688-naive-sdf-generation-cpu.md) overhead. See [GPU-Based Dynamic LOD Calculation](10845-gpu-based-dynamic-lod-calculation.md).

### [Histogram Spectra for LOD Selection](11687-histogram-spectra-for-lod-selection.md)
[Histogram Spectra for LOD Selection](#11687-histogram-spectra-for-lod-selection.md) (HSPE) is a metadata-driven technique for selecting Level of Detail (LOD) in multivariate, time-varying volume rendering. It solves the problem of interactive LOD selection for large, out-of-core volumes by precomputing statistical sensitivity metrics, allowing error estimation without accessing the raw volume data. Unlike direct RMS error computation which requires reading the entire dataset, HSPE uses compact histogram spectra to pose LOD selection as an integer programming problem, maximizing quality within a working set size constraint. See [Histogram Spectra for LOD Selection](11687-histogram-spectra-for-lod-selection.md).

### [LOD Assignment Algorithm](11688-lod-assignment-algorithm.md)
The [LOD Assignment Algorithm](#11688-lod-assignment-algorithm.md) is a method for assigning levels of detail (LOD) to subvolumes in a [volume rendering pipeline](#1318-volume-rendering-pipeline.md) to minimize visual error density subject to a maximum working set size constraint ($S_{max}$). It solves the problem of fitting a high-resolution volume dataset into limited memory or bandwidth by selecting the coarsest possible resolution for each spatial block while maintaining acceptable quality. It sets itself apart from sibling methods like [Hierarchical Culling & Multi-resolution Approximation](2010-hierarchical-culling-multi-resolution-approximation.md) by explicitly optimizing for error density per byte rather than just geometric distance or simple thresholding, and differs from [Streaming and Level-of-Detail (LOD) selection](3087-streaming-and-level-of-detail-lod-selection.md) by using a global constraint on the total working set size rather than local streaming buffers. See [LOD Assignment Algorithm](11688-lod-assignment-algorithm.md).

### LoD Selection via Projected Width
This variant uses the projected width of a voxel or primitive on the camera plane to determine the required LOD level, following usual PathTracer MipMap selection logic [S1]. It involves loading multiple computed LoD volumes simultaneously (one per LoD level) and choosing which volume to lookup for data at each voxel based on the required LoD level [S1].

### Hybrid LoD
This variant combines multiple LOD strategies to optimize quality and performance. On the Helmet scene at $32^3$ resolution, HybridLoD achieves an [RMSE](#10453-depth-accuracy-metrics.md) of 0.266 / 0.302 and renders in 1.0 second [S2, unofficial].

### Transfer Function Based Level-of-Detail (LOD)
This method classifies block content as Empty (all voxels transparent), Homogeneous (non-transparent voxels, similar color), or Varying (varying transparency, varying color) [S3, unofficial]. Block significance is based on visual error calculated as color difference from CIE L*u*v*, denoted as $\Delta E$ [S3, unofficial]. It achieved a data reduction of 64:1 (1.6% error, 2.25 MB) on a 144 MB, $512 \times 512 \times 384$ volume [S3, unofficial].

## Background
LOD selection and culling are fundamental techniques in volume rendering, originating from the need to handle the computational complexity of raycasting and texture-based rendering on large datasets. Early work focused on hierarchical structures like octrees and bricks to enable frustum culling and resolution selection based on distance [S1][S2, unofficial]. The introduction of GPU-based rendering accelerated the adoption of dynamic LOD calculation, allowing for real-time adjustments based on screen-space error and projected size [S1][S2, unofficial]. Recent developments include temporal coherence to prevent flickering [S1], metadata-driven selection using histogram spectra for out-of-core volumes [S1], and hybrid approaches that combine geometric and appearance-based metrics [S2, unofficial].
